title: For the ways of peace (Gittin 61a)
hook: the Talmud rules that poor non-Jews are fed and their sick visited, for the ways of peace

segments.voice: Yesterday, the page is open: Beruriah reading closely, and a page of Talmud that asks only to be read. Did you say your sentence to a learner? Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

Feed the poor. Visit the sick. Bury the dead. Familiar duties, done by neighbors, by burial societies, by the person who brings soup. The Talmud takes that list and adds a few words that change its size. Not only for the Jewish poor, the Jewish sick, the Jewish dead. For non-Jews too, side by side with them. And it gives a reason in one short Hebrew phrase. Today's word is that reason.
screen: `FEED, VISIT, BURY.` → `NOT ONLY YOUR OWN.` → `SIDE BY SIDE.`

segments.voice: For the ways of peace. In Hebrew, mipnei darkhei shalom. First, the ruling. In tractate Gittin, the Talmud brings a teaching: the poor of non-Jews are supported along with the poor of Israel, their sick are visited along with the sick of Israel, and their dead are buried along with the dead of Israel, for the ways of peace. Along with. Not after. Not instead. In the same rounds, at the same tables. Second, a phrase with a family. The Mishnah in the same tractate lists other rulings made for the ways of peace. The Torah reading in synagogue goes first to a priest, then a Levite, then any other Jew, so nobody quarrels over who goes first. And poor non-Jews are not stopped from gleaning in the fields. Small rules that keep a shared street calm. Third, the size of it. The Talmud goes further, and says the whole Torah is for the sake of the ways of peace. Its proof is a verse from Proverbs about wisdom and Torah: "Her ways are ways of pleasantness, and all her paths are peace." Fourth, two ways to hear it. Some readers hear the phrase as practical wisdom: neighbors who are cared for stay neighbors. Others, Maimonides among them, tie these rulings to a verse in the Psalms saying that God is good to all and has mercy on all his works, and to the Proverbs verse, as if to say the law is simply acting like its Giver. Both readings live in the tradition. Either way, the soup goes to every door on the street.
screen: `FEED, VISIT, BURY: ALONG WITH ISRAEL.` · `SMALL RULES FOR A SHARED STREET.` · `ALL HER PATHS ARE PEACE.` · `PRACTICAL WISDOM, OR GOD'S OWN WAY?` · then, large: `FOR THE WAYS OF PEACE.`

segments.voice: Today's practice is to help someone outside your circle. Settle, and let your breath slow. Picture your circle: family, friends, the people who share your faith or your table. Now let your attention drift to its edge. A neighbor you only nod to. The person who delivers your packages. A coworker you've never really spoken with. Someone of another faith, or none. Let one face come forward. Ask what small thing might help them this week. A meal. A visit. A word. Hold the face, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
For the ways of peace. Mipnei darkhei shalom: the Talmud's reason for feeding, visiting and burying non-Jews along with Jews. Today's word.
screen: `FOR THE WAYS OF PEACE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: for the ways of peace. Today, do one small kindness for someone outside your usual circle, and do it the Talmud's way: along with, not after. Day one thousand one hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Jewish food pantries, visiting committees and charities often serve neighbors of every background, and some cite the ruling 'for the ways of peace' as one reason.
